member.name: T:DotNetCore.HayateOP.Buffers.HayateBufferPool`1
member.summary: A bucketed array pool: a fixed ladder of size buckets, where each rent request routes — rounded up to the nearest bucket — to the smallest bucket whose arrays can hold it, and a returned array parks in its home bucket until the bucket's capacity is full.
member.remarks:
Scope note: this is the one piece of surface the core pool deliberately does not carry, because for most .NET workloads System.Buffers.ArrayPool<T> already covers it. This pool exists for callers who want that shape under an explicit, inspectable configuration — the bucket ladder is declared up front, every bucket's retained count is fixed by declaration, and nothing sizes or trims buckets behind the caller's back. It is the aligned counterpart of TinyPools' MemoryPool<T> + SegmentDefinition, under HayateOP naming and validation conventions.
Routing is "round up to the nearest declared size": a request is served by the first bucket whose covers it, so the caller receives an array at least as long as requested and never has to grow. A request above the largest declared size is rejected with rather than served by an undeclared bucket — the ladder is exactly what was configured, nothing more.
Buckets create arrays on demand and cap only what they retain: any number of buffers may be outstanding at once, and returns past a bucket's are dropped for the garbage collector. There is no background worker of any kind — an idle pool holds its declared buckets and runs nothing.
The pool is thread-safe: each bucket guards its parking stack with its own lock, so different bucket sizes do not contend.
member.typeparam: The element type of the pooled arrays.

member.name: T:DotNetCore.HayateOP.Buffers.PooledBuffer`1
member.summary: A buffer rented from a : a array whose length is the renting bucket's fixed size, handed back to its bucket by .
member.remarks:
The handle exists so the using pattern returns the buffer — the pool never takes a bare array back, because it could not tell which bucket a caller-modified array belongs to. A handle is single-use: disposing it twice, or returning it through the pool after disposing, is a no-op, so a using block and a manual Return never fight over the same buffer.
The array's previous contents are not cleared on return — the same contract ArrayPool<T>.Shared has. Inspect only the elements you wrote, or clear the buffer yourself if the next reader could otherwise observe stale data.
